implementation_notes: mockgen generates Mock implementations from interfaces (source, package or archive mode) and gomock.NewController(t) ties expectation checking to the test's lifetime: EXPECT().HasInventory(gomock.Eq("Talisker"), gomock.Eq(50)).Return(true) states the expected call, Times/After constrain cardinality and order, and the controller fails the test on a missing or unexpected call. Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly, so the double needs no inheritance; a hand-written expectation struct is only better for a single trivial call or when code generation is not allowed in the build.
pitfalls: The generated mock must be regenerated when the interface changes: without a //go:generate or build step a stale mock either fails to compile or silently misses new methods.
Expectations are checked through the controller tied to *testing.T (or a TestReporter); reusing one controller across tests attributes failures to the wrong test.
Expectations are order-independent unless .After()/InOrder is used, and a mock with zero EXPECT() calls asserts nothing - the test can pass while the interaction is never exercised.

variants.name: testify/mock hand-written forwarders
variants.implementation_notes: testify/mock keeps the double in your code but standardises the plumbing: the test type embeds mock.Mock, each interface method forwards m.Called(args...) and extracts typed results, while the test programmes On("Remove", "Talisker", 50).Return() and finishes with AssertExpectations(t). Choose it when the project already uses testify's assert/require packages or when a build step for mockgen is unwelcome.
pitfalls: Every method needs a hand-written forwarder; an interface method that is not forwarded calls the embedded Mock's own method set and panics or returns zero values.
AssertExpectations must be called explicitly - without it the On() expectations are never checked and unmet calls pass unnoticed.
